title: What Caught My Attention When Jensen Huang Returned to Nvidia
author: O
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The most interesting part of the Jensen Huang story isn’t the boardroom decision. It’s the employee reaction.

When Huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters, employees cheered and chanted his name. Some watched from the floors above. The next day, at an all-hands meeting, Huang apologized to staff and acknowledged that he had violated aspects of the company’s code of conduct.

What struck me about the footage was how personal the welcome felt. A board can reinstate a CEO with a vote. Employees decide for themselves how they feel about seeing that person walk back through the door. The people who gathered to cheer made their feelings clear. Others may have experienced the same week very differently.

In semiconductors, loyalty often grows out of years spent working through complex technical challenges together. After 45 years in the semiconductor industry I have experienced this many times. Nvidia’s engineers have spent years building a platform that spans chips, networking, and software. The people doing that work see up close how priorities get set, how disagreements get resolved, and who backs a team when it takes a risk. That daily experience helps explain why a founder’s return can mean something personal to employees.

It also makes Huang’s comments about succession worth revisiting. He told staff that Nvidia already has capable leaders running different parts of the business. The question is how those leaders would make decisions together when the person they are accustomed to turning to is unavailable.

We will all be watching what happens in the quieter weeks ahead. Can employees who cheered his return and employees who had reservations both feel comfortable challenging him in a meeting? Can senior leaders make tough calls and know Huang will back them? Those are the everyday tests of trust inside Nvidia, long after the cameras have left the lobby.
